questiontext.text: What is the core idea of property-based testing (PBT)?

answer.text: Instead of hand-writing example inputs, you state a property (a predicate expected to hold for all valid inputs) and a framework generates many random inputs trying to falsify it

feedback.text: Correct — PBT checks a general property against many auto-generated inputs.

answer.text: It formally proves that the program meets its complete specification

feedback.text: PBT can find counterexamples but does not prove correctness.

answer.text: It measures how many branches a fixed test suite covers

feedback.text: That is coverage measurement; PBT is about generating inputs to check a property.

answer.text: It runs a single fixed input many times to check for flakiness

feedback.text: PBT varies the input across a whole space, not one fixed input repeated.

generalfeedback.text: In property-based testing you describe a property that should hold for every input, and the framework (QuickCheck, Hypothesis, fast-check, ScalaCheck) generates many random inputs to try to break it. A properties-over-a-space approach complements example tests, which check individual points.

questiontext.text: In PBT, what is a property?

answer.text: A predicate about the code's behavior that should hold for every valid input (e.g. "the output list is always sorted")

feedback.text: Correct — a property is a rule expected to hold across all inputs.

answer.text: A single input paired with its exact expected output

feedback.text: That describes an example (unit) test case, not a property.

answer.text: A measurement of the program's running time

feedback.text: That is a performance metric, not a correctness property.

answer.text: The random seed used to reproduce a run

feedback.text: A seed concerns reproducibility, not the predicate being checked.

generalfeedback.text: A property is a universally-quantified statement about the code: it should hold for all inputs the generator can produce. Examples include round-trip, invariant, idempotence, and commutativity properties. The framework searches for an input that violates it.

questiontext.text: What is a generator (also called an arbitrary) in PBT?

answer.text: A recipe that produces random values of a given type to feed as test inputs

feedback.text: Correct — generators supply the random inputs the property is checked against.

answer.text: The exact expected output computed for each input

feedback.text: A generator makes inputs, not expected outputs.

answer.text: The property predicate that must hold

feedback.text: The predicate is the property; the generator produces the inputs it is tested on.

answer.text: The function under test itself

feedback.text: The generator feeds inputs to the function under test; it is not that function.

generalfeedback.text: A generator (arbitrary) knows how to construct random values of a type — integers, strings, lists, records, trees. The framework draws many values from it and checks the property on each. Generators can be composed and constrained to shape the distribution of inputs.

questiontext.text: What is shrinking in property-based testing?

answer.text: When a random input falsifies the property, the framework automatically reduces it to a smaller, minimal input that still fails, making the counterexample easier to understand

feedback.text: Correct — shrinking searches for a minimal still-failing input.

answer.text: It deletes tests that pass to make the report shorter

feedback.text: Shrinking reduces a failing input, not the set of passing tests.

answer.text: It compresses the test-output log file on disk

feedback.text: Shrinking is about simplifying a counterexample, not compressing files.

answer.text: It lowers the number of generated inputs to make the run faster

feedback.text: That would be reducing the case count; shrinking instead minimizes a discovered failing input.

generalfeedback.text: A randomly found counterexample is often large and noisy. Shrinking repeatedly tries simpler variants (shorter lists, smaller numbers) and keeps only those that still fail, converging on a minimal failing input. This makes the root cause far easier to see, which is why shrinking speeds debugging.

questiontext.text: What is a counterexample in PBT?

answer.text: A concrete input for which the property fails, demonstrating a defect

feedback.text: Correct — a counterexample is a witnessing input that violates the property.

answer.text: An input for which the property holds

feedback.text: An input that holds is a passing case, not a counterexample.

answer.text: The expected output value for a chosen input

feedback.text: A counterexample is an input that breaks the property, not an expected output.

answer.text: A hand-written example test that passes

feedback.text: A passing example is not a counterexample; a counterexample falsifies the property.

generalfeedback.text: When the framework finds an input that makes the property false, that input is a counterexample: proof that the code (or the property) is wrong. The framework then shrinks it to a minimal form and reports it, along with the seed for reproduction.

questiontext.text: How does a property-based test differ from a traditional example-based (unit) test?

answer.text: An example test checks one specific input-output point; a property test checks a rule across a whole space of generated inputs

feedback.text: Correct — examples cover points, properties cover a space.

answer.text: They are identical; both check one fixed input against one expected value

feedback.text: A property test generates many inputs and checks a general rule, unlike a single example.

answer.text: A property test needs the exact expected output for every generated input

feedback.text: A property states a rule that avoids needing a per-input expected value.

answer.text: An example test generates random inputs while a property test uses fixed ones

feedback.text: It is the reverse: property tests generate inputs; example tests use fixed ones.

generalfeedback.text: Example tests pin down specific, important points ("f(2) == 4"). Property tests state a rule ("for all x, f(x) >= 0") and let a generator explore many inputs. The two are complementary: examples are precise regressions, properties give broad coverage.

questiontext.text: What are QuickCheck, Hypothesis, fast-check, and ScalaCheck?

answer.text: Property-based testing frameworks (for Haskell, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Scala respectively)

feedback.text: Correct — these are PBT libraries for different languages.

answer.text: Code coverage measurement tools

feedback.text: They are PBT frameworks, not coverage tools.

answer.text: Static type checkers

feedback.text: They run tests with generated inputs; they are not type checkers.

answer.text: Continuous-integration build systems

feedback.text: They are testing libraries, not CI/build systems.

generalfeedback.text: QuickCheck (Haskell) pioneered the approach; Hypothesis (Python), fast-check (JS/TS), and ScalaCheck (Scala) bring the same idea to other languages: declare properties and generators, and the tool generates inputs and shrinks failures.

questiontext.text: Which is a valid property of a correct list reverse function?

answer.text: reverse(reverse(xs)) == xs for all lists xs

feedback.text: Correct — reversing twice returns the original list (reverse is its own inverse).

answer.text: reverse(xs) == xs for all lists xs

feedback.text: That holds only for palindromic lists, not all lists.

answer.text: reverse(xs) has a different length from xs

feedback.text: Reversing preserves the length; it only changes the order.

answer.text: reverse(xs) doubles the list

feedback.text: Reverse rearranges the same elements; it does not add any.

generalfeedback.text: Reverse is an involution: applying it twice yields the original list, so reverse(reverse(xs)) == xs is a valid round-trip property. Note reverse(xs) == xs is false in general (only palindromes satisfy it), which makes it a good distractor.

questiontext.text: A function f is idempotent when which property holds for all x?

feedback.text: Correct — applying an idempotent function again changes nothing after the first application.

answer.text: f(x) == x

feedback.text: That is the identity function, a stricter and different condition.

answer.text: f(a, b) == f(b, a)

feedback.text: That is commutativity, not idempotence.

answer.text: f(f(x)) == x

feedback.text: That is involution (self-inverse), such as reverse or negate, not idempotence.

generalfeedback.text: Idempotence means f(f(x)) == f(x): once applied, applying again has no further effect. Examples include sort, abs, and normalize. It differs from the identity (f(x) == x) and from involution (f(f(x)) == x, e.g. reverse).

questiontext.text: A round-trip (inverse) property for an encode/decode pair states which of the following?

answer.text: decode(encode(x)) == x for all x

feedback.text: Correct — encoding then decoding must return the original value.

answer.text: encode(x) == decode(x) for all x

feedback.text: Encode and decode are inverses, not equal functions.

answer.text: encode(x) == x for all x

feedback.text: Encoding transforms the value; it does not leave it unchanged.

answer.text: decode(x) == x for all x

feedback.text: Decoding is the inverse of encoding, not the identity.

generalfeedback.text: A round-trip property says that decoding undoes encoding: decode(encode(x)) == x for every value x. This is a very common and powerful property for serializers, codecs, and parser/printer pairs, because it needs no per-input expected value.

questiontext.text: Why do PBT frameworks report a random seed with a failure?

answer.text: Recording the seed lets you re-run the exact same generated inputs to reproduce the failure deterministically

feedback.text: Correct — the seed makes a random run reproducible.

answer.text: The seed is the expected output of the failing test

feedback.text: The seed drives the random generator; it is not an expected output.

answer.text: The seed measures how much code the test covered

feedback.text: Coverage is separate; the seed only controls input generation.

answer.text: The seed proves the property holds for all inputs

feedback.text: A seed reproduces one run; it proves nothing about all inputs.

generalfeedback.text: Random generation would be hard to debug if every run differed. Frameworks seed their random source and report the seed on failure, so you can replay the identical sequence of inputs and reproduce (and then fix) the bug reliably.

name.text: A passing run does not prove correctness

questiontext.text: If a property-based test runs thousands of random inputs and finds no counterexample, the property is thereby proven to hold for all possible inputs.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — a passing run only means no counterexample was found among the generated inputs, not that none exists.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — PBT samples finitely many inputs; a clean run raises confidence but does not prove the property.

generalfeedback.text: Like testing in general, PBT can show the presence of faults (a counterexample) but not their absence. The input space is usually unbounded, and only finitely many inputs are tried, so a passing run is strong evidence, not a proof.

questiontext.text: When shrinking a failing input, the framework only reports a reduced input that still causes the property to fail.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a shrink candidate is kept only if it still triggers the failure.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Shrinking preserves the failure: it never reports a reduced input that passes.

generalfeedback.text: Shrinking explores simpler variants of the failing input but discards any candidate that no longer fails. The final reported counterexample is a minimal input that still violates the property, so it does not change the pass/fail verdict.

questiontext.text: Which is a valid property of a correct abs (absolute value) function over the reals?

answer.text: abs(x) >= 0 for all x

feedback.text: Correct — an absolute value is never negative.

answer.text: abs(x) > 0 for all x

feedback.text: Fails at x = 0, where abs(0) = 0, which is not greater than 0.

answer.text: abs(x) == x for all x

feedback.text: Holds only for non-negative x; fails for negative x.

answer.text: abs(x) == -x for all x

feedback.text: Holds only for non-positive x; fails for positive x.

generalfeedback.text: abs(x) >= 0 holds for every real x, so it is a valid property. Note abs(x) > 0 is subtly wrong because of x = 0, and both abs(x) == x and abs(x) == -x are true only on half the domain. A stronger property is abs(-x) == abs(x).

questiontext.text: For map(f, xs) (apply f to each element of a list), which is a valid property?

answer.text: len(map(f, xs)) == len(xs) for all lists xs

feedback.text: Correct — mapping preserves length; it transforms elements one-for-one.

answer.text: len(map(f, xs)) == 0 for all lists xs

feedback.text: Mapping keeps every element, so the length is unchanged, not zero.

answer.text: len(map(f, xs)) == 2 * len(xs) for all lists xs

feedback.text: Mapping is one-to-one; it does not double the length.

answer.text: map reverses the order of the elements

feedback.text: Map preserves order; each element is transformed in place.

generalfeedback.text: map applies f to each element without adding, dropping, or reordering elements, so len(map(f, xs)) == len(xs) is a valid length-preservation invariant — a simple structural property that holds regardless of f.

questiontext.text: You are testing a serialize function and its matching parse function. Which is the best single property to check?

answer.text: parse(serialize(x)) == x for all values x (round-trip)

feedback.text: Correct — serializing then parsing must recover the original value.

answer.text: serialize(x) is a non-empty string for all x

feedback.text: True but far too weak — it says nothing about recovering x.

answer.text: parse(serialize(x)) does not throw an exception

feedback.text: Not crashing is weak; it allows a wrong parsed value to pass.

answer.text: serialize(x) == serialize(x)

feedback.text: That is trivially true and tests nothing.

generalfeedback.text: The round-trip property parse(serialize(x)) == x pins down the essential contract: the pair is a faithful inverse. The distractors are either tautologies or so weak that a broken implementation could still satisfy them.

questiontext.text: Which property fully captures correctness of a sort function?

answer.text: The output is in non-decreasing order AND is a permutation (same multiset of elements) of the input

feedback.text: Correct — ordering plus the permutation condition together specify a correct sort.

answer.text: The output is in non-decreasing order

feedback.text: Insufficient alone — returning [] is ordered but wrong; you also need the permutation condition.

answer.text: The output has the same length as the input

feedback.text: Necessary but far from sufficient; wrong elements of the right length would pass.

answer.text: The output's sum equals the input's sum

feedback.text: Necessary but insufficient — e.g. input [1,3] and output [2,2] share a sum yet [2,2] is not a permutation.

generalfeedback.text: A correct sort must be ordered and must contain exactly the same elements (as a multiset) as the input. Checking only ordering, only length, or only the sum each admits wrong implementations. The permutation (multiset-equality) condition is the indispensable second half.

questiontext.text: Why is "the output is sorted" insufficient as the only property for a sort function?

answer.text: A broken implementation that returns [] (or drops/duplicates elements) still produces sorted output and passes; you must also require the output to be a permutation of the input

feedback.text: Correct — "return []" trivially satisfies "is sorted", so the permutation condition is essential.

answer.text: Because a correct sort is not always ordered

feedback.text: A correct sort is always ordered; ordering is necessary, just not sufficient.

answer.text: Because checking order is computationally impossible

feedback.text: Checking order is trivial; the issue is that order alone permits wrong outputs.

answer.text: Because sorting has no checkable properties

feedback.text: Sorting has strong properties; ordered plus permutation together specify it.

generalfeedback.text: The empty list is sorted, so a function that always returns [] passes an "is sorted" check while being completely wrong. So do functions that drop or duplicate elements. Adding the permutation (multiset) requirement rules these out — a classic lesson in choosing a sufficient property.

questiontext.text: A function normalize converts a string to a canonical form (e.g. Unicode NFC, trim, lowercase). Which property should hold?

answer.text: normalize(normalize(s)) == normalize(s) for all s (idempotence)

feedback.text: Correct — normalizing an already-normalized string changes nothing.

answer.text: normalize(s) == s for all s

feedback.text: False — normalizing a non-canonical string changes it.

answer.text: normalize(normalize(s)) == s for all s

feedback.text: That is involution, which does not hold: the first normalize may already have altered s.

answer.text: len(normalize(s)) == len(s) for all s

feedback.text: Trimming or Unicode composition can change the length, so this is false.

generalfeedback.text: Canonicalization is idempotent: once a string is in canonical form, normalizing again leaves it unchanged, so normalize(normalize(s)) == normalize(s). It is not the identity (it can change s) and not an involution (it cannot recover the original from the canonical form).

name.text: What shrinking reports for a failing list

questiontext.text: A property fails on the randomly generated list [7, -3, 0, 12, 5, -8, 4]. What will a shrinking-capable framework typically report?

answer.text: A minimized input that still fails — for instance the shortest/simplest list (perhaps a single element or [ ]) that reproduces the failure

feedback.text: Correct — shrinking converges on a minimal still-failing input.

answer.text: The original seven-element list, unchanged

feedback.text: Shrinking works to reduce the input rather than report it as-is.

answer.text: An input that now passes the property

feedback.text: Shrinking never reports a passing input; the reduced input must still fail.

answer.text: A completely different random list unrelated to the failure

feedback.text: Shrinking simplifies the failing input; it does not switch to an unrelated one.

generalfeedback.text: Shrinking repeatedly tries simpler versions (drop elements, reduce magnitudes) and keeps only those that still fail, ending at a minimal counterexample. This isolates the essential trigger and makes debugging far quicker than staring at the original noisy input.

name.text: Reproducing a CI failure via seed

questiontext.text: A CI run reports a property failure together with a seed. To debug it locally, what should a developer do?

answer.text: Re-run the test with the same seed to regenerate the identical inputs and reproduce the failure

feedback.text: Correct — replaying the seed reproduces the exact failing run.

answer.text: Increase the number of generated cases and hope it recurs

feedback.text: Unreliable — the seed already lets you reproduce it exactly, without guessing.

answer.text: Disable shrinking so the test stops failing

feedback.text: Disabling shrinking hides the minimal counterexample; it does not fix or reproduce anything.

answer.text: Change the property until the test passes

feedback.text: That masks the bug rather than diagnosing it.

generalfeedback.text: The seed captures the exact random choices of a run. Re-running with it deterministically regenerates the same (already shrunk) inputs, so the developer sees the identical failure locally and can step through it.

questiontext.text: For which function f is the property f(f(x)) == f(x) valid for all x?

answer.text: Taking the absolute value: abs

feedback.text: Correct — abs(abs(x)) == abs(x), so abs is idempotent.

answer.text: Incrementing by one: inc(x) = x + 1

feedback.text: Not idempotent — inc(inc(x)) = x + 2, which differs from inc(x) = x + 1.

answer.text: Reversing a list: reverse

feedback.text: Reverse is an involution (reverse(reverse(x)) == x), not idempotent.

answer.text: Negating a number: neg(x) = -x

feedback.text: Negation is an involution (neg(neg(x)) == x), not idempotent.

generalfeedback.text: abs is idempotent because once a value is non-negative, taking abs again does nothing. Increment fails (adds 2 vs 1), and reverse/negate are involutions (applying twice returns the original), which is a different property.

questiontext.text: Which operation satisfies a valid commutativity property f(a, b) == f(b, a) for all inputs?

answer.text: Multiplication: a * b == b * a

feedback.text: Correct — multiplication is commutative.

answer.text: Subtraction: a - b == b - a

feedback.text: False in general — e.g. 5 - 3 = 2 but 3 - 5 = -2.

answer.text: Division: a / b == b / a

feedback.text: False in general — e.g. 6 / 2 = 3 but 2 / 6 ≈ 0.33.

answer.text: Exponentiation: a ** b == b ** a

feedback.text: False in general — e.g. 2 ** 3 = 8 but 3 ** 2 = 9.

generalfeedback.text: Commutativity, f(a, b) == f(b, a), holds for addition and multiplication but not for subtraction, division, or exponentiation. Choosing a commutativity property for a non-commutative operation would flag correct code.

name.text: Round-trip property for a base64 codec

questiontext.text: For a base64 codec, which round-trip property is the correct one to check?

answer.text: decode(encode(bytes)) == bytes, generating random byte sequences

feedback.text: Correct — encoding arbitrary bytes then decoding must recover them exactly.

answer.text: encode(decode(s)) == s, generating random strings s

feedback.text: Unsound — a random string need not be valid/canonical base64, so this can fail on correct code.

answer.text: encode(bytes) == bytes for all byte sequences

feedback.text: Encoding transforms bytes into text; it does not return the input unchanged.

answer.text: decode(encode(bytes)) is shorter than bytes

feedback.text: The round trip returns the original bytes, so it is the same length, not shorter.

generalfeedback.text: Generate the raw values (bytes), encode, then decode: decode(encode(bytes)) == bytes is sound because every byte sequence is encodable. The reverse direction over random strings is a classic trap: not every string is a valid base64 encoding, so encode(decode(s)) == s can legitimately fail.

name.text: Using a reference implementation as an oracle

questiontext.text: You have a fast but complex implementation fast_fn and a slow but obviously-correct reference ref_fn of the same specification. How can PBT use the reference?

answer.text: Generate random inputs and assert fast_fn(x) == ref_fn(x) — the reference acts as the test oracle

feedback.text: Correct — comparing against a trusted reference gives an oracle for free.

answer.text: Assert fast_fn(x) == fast_fn(x) for random x

feedback.text: That is trivially true and tests nothing.

answer.text: Replace fast_fn with ref_fn in production

feedback.text: The reference is a testing oracle, not a production replacement (it is slow).

answer.text: Only test inputs where the two already agree

feedback.text: That defeats the purpose — you want to find inputs where they disagree.

generalfeedback.text: A simpler reference implementation is an excellent oracle: for each generated input, the optimized version must match it. This is "test oracle from a simpler model" and is the basis of differential/model-based testing. Any disagreement is a counterexample that shrinking then minimizes.

questiontext.text: To check that a sort output is a permutation of the input, which check is correct?

answer.text: The output and input have equal element multisets (each value occurs the same number of times in both)

feedback.text: Correct — multiset equality captures the permutation condition.

answer.text: The output and input have the same length

feedback.text: Same length is necessary but not sufficient; the elements could differ.

answer.text: The output and input have the same first element

feedback.text: The first elements can differ (the smallest need not be first in the input), and this ignores the rest.

answer.text: The output and input have the same sum

feedback.text: Equal sums do not imply equal multisets — [1,3] and [2,2] share a sum but differ.

generalfeedback.text: A permutation preserves the multiset of elements: comparing element counts (or comparing sorted-by-a-trusted-method versions) verifies it. Length or sum equality are weaker consequences that many wrong outputs also satisfy.

questiontext.text: Why do PBT frameworks let you inspect the distribution of generated inputs (e.g. Hypothesis statistics, QuickCheck's collect/classify)?

answer.text: To confirm the generator actually produces the interesting and edge cases; a skewed generator may never exercise the inputs that trigger a bug

feedback.text: Correct — distribution insight guards against a generator that misses important cases.

answer.text: To measure statement and branch coverage of the code

feedback.text: That is code coverage, a separate concern from input distribution.

answer.text: To make shrinking run faster

feedback.text: Distribution reporting informs generation quality, not shrinking speed.

answer.text: To prove the property holds on all inputs

feedback.text: No sampling proves a universal property; distribution stats only describe what was generated.

generalfeedback.text: If a generator rarely (or never) produces empty lists, boundary numbers, or duplicates, a property can pass while the bug-triggering inputs are never tried. Distribution reporting lets you verify — and tune — that the important regions of the input space are actually being sampled.

questiontext.text: Checking only that a sort function's output is in non-decreasing order is a complete property that fully verifies sorting.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — a function returning [] is ordered but wrong; you also need the permutation (multiset) condition.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — ordering alone is satisfied by wrong implementations; the output must also be a permutation of the input.

generalfeedback.text: "Is sorted" is necessary but not sufficient. Returning an empty list, or dropping/duplicating elements, yields ordered output yet is incorrect. A complete sort property pairs ordering with multiset equality between input and output.

questiontext.text: For a function dedup(xs) that removes duplicate values from a list, which is a valid invariant property?

answer.text: dedup(xs) contains no repeated value, and its set of elements equals the set of elements of xs

feedback.text: Correct — deduplication removes repeats while preserving exactly which values are present.

answer.text: len(dedup(xs)) == len(xs) for all xs

feedback.text: False when xs has duplicates; the length must drop in that case.

answer.text: dedup(xs) == xs for all xs

feedback.text: Holds only when xs already has no duplicates, not for all lists.

answer.text: dedup preserves the count of each value

feedback.text: Deduplication collapses repeats to one occurrence, so per-value counts are not preserved.

generalfeedback.text: A correct dedup output has no repeats and covers exactly the same distinct values as the input — i.e. equal element sets, plus a "no duplicates" invariant. Length is preserved only when there were no duplicates, and per-value counts are deliberately not preserved.

questiontext.text: Which property expresses that sorting is idempotent?

answer.text: sort(sort(xs)) == sort(xs) for all lists xs

feedback.text: Correct — sorting an already-sorted list leaves it unchanged.

answer.text: sort(sort(xs)) == xs for all lists xs

feedback.text: False in general — the inner sort reorders xs, so you do not recover the original.

answer.text: sort(xs) == xs for all lists xs

feedback.text: True only when xs is already sorted, not for all lists.

answer.text: sort(xs) reverses an already-sorted list

feedback.text: Sorting never reverses a sorted list; it leaves it in order.

generalfeedback.text: Idempotence for sort means applying it again has no effect: sort(sort(xs)) == sort(xs). Note this alone is a weak property (many wrong functions are idempotent); it complements, but does not replace, ordering plus permutation.

questiontext.text: A tester proposes encode(decode(s)) == s as the round-trip property for a codec, generating random strings s. Why can this raise false failures on correct code?

answer.text: Not every random string is a valid/canonical encoding, so decode may reject or canonicalize it and encode(decode(s)) need not equal s; the sound property is decode(encode(x)) == x over generated decoded values x

feedback.text: Correct — the generated strings need not lie in the range of encode, so the direction is unsound.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; it always holds for a correct codec

feedback.text: It fails whenever s is not a canonical encoding, even for correct codecs.

answer.text: Codecs cannot be tested with PBT at all

feedback.text: They can — the sound direction decode(encode(x)) == x is a strong property.

answer.text: The random seed is chosen incorrectly

feedback.text: The issue is the property's direction, not the seed.

generalfeedback.text: encode(decode(s)) == s only holds when s is already a canonical output of encode. Random strings often are not (non-canonical padding, extra whitespace), so a correct codec can violate it. Generate the source values and check decode(encode(x)) == x instead — encode's range is exactly what decode must invert.

name.text: A proposed property that is actually false

questiontext.text: A tester writes the property inc(inc(n)) == inc(n) for an increment function inc(n) = n + 1. What happens?

answer.text: The property is false for a correct inc (inc(inc(n)) = n + 2 ≠ n + 1), so PBT quickly finds a counterexample — but it signals a wrong property, not a bug in inc

feedback.text: Correct — the property mistakenly assumes idempotence; the failure is the property's fault.

answer.text: It correctly verifies that inc works

feedback.text: It does not — a correct inc violates this false property.

answer.text: It proves inc is idempotent

feedback.text: inc is not idempotent; the property is simply wrong.

answer.text: It passes for all n

feedback.text: It fails for every n, since n + 2 is never n + 1.

generalfeedback.text: Increment is not idempotent: applying it twice adds 2. Writing an idempotence property for it asserts something false, so the framework reports a counterexample. The lesson: a failing PBT run can mean the property is wrong, so validate that each asserted property genuinely holds for a correct implementation.

questiontext.text: What characterizes stateful (model-based) property-based testing?

answer.text: The framework generates random sequences of commands, runs them against both the real system and a simplified model, and asserts the observable results agree after each step; failing sequences are then shrunk

feedback.text: Correct — model-based PBT compares a system against a reference model over command sequences.

answer.text: It tests a single pure function on random inputs with no state

feedback.text: That is ordinary (stateless) PBT; model-based PBT drives stateful systems.

answer.text: It measures how many states the program reaches

feedback.text: That is a coverage notion, not model-based checking of behavior.

answer.text: It replaces the real database with random data and does nothing else

feedback.text: Randomizing data is not the point; comparing the system to a model over command sequences is.

generalfeedback.text: Model-based PBT generates a random program (a sequence of operations), executes it against the real system and against a simple correct-by-inspection model, and checks that observations match at every step. When a sequence disagrees, shrinking reduces it to a minimal failing command sequence — the essence of the bug.

name.text: Value of shrinking a large structured input

questiontext.text: A property fails on a randomly generated 500-node tree with particular values. Why is shrinking especially valuable here?

answer.text: It reduces the huge failing input to a minimal still-failing structure (e.g. a two- or three-node tree), isolating the essential trigger and greatly speeding debugging — without changing the fail verdict

feedback.text: Correct — shrinking distills a large counterexample down to its core.

answer.text: It proves the property holds on all smaller trees

feedback.text: Shrinking finds a minimal failing case; it proves nothing about passing cases.

answer.text: It makes the original 500-node tree pass

feedback.text: Shrinking does not alter verdicts; the input still fails.

answer.text: It converts the tree into a list to simplify the type

feedback.text: Shrinking preserves the input's type/structure; it reduces size, not the type.

generalfeedback.text: A 500-node counterexample is nearly impossible to reason about. Shrinking prunes nodes and reduces values while keeping the failure, often arriving at a tiny structure that exposes the exact condition. This is where shrinking pays off most, and it never changes whether the input fails.

questiontext.text: A generator for testing a "parse a non-negative integer" function only ever produces 3-to-5-digit numeric strings. What is the risk?

answer.text: It may never generate boundary and edge inputs (empty string, leading zeros, non-numeric characters, very large values), so bugs on those go undetected and a passing run gives false confidence

feedback.text: Correct — a narrow generator leaves whole regions of the input space untested.

answer.text: Shrinking will stop working entirely

feedback.text: Shrinking still works within the generated range; the problem is the range is too narrow.

answer.text: The recorded seed becomes invalid

feedback.text: The seed remains valid; the concern is coverage of the input space.

answer.text: The property automatically becomes false

feedback.text: The property is unchanged; it is just under-exercised.

generalfeedback.text: The bugs in a parser usually hide at the edges — empty input, leading zeros, non-digits, overflow-sized numbers. A generator that only emits typical mid-range values never reaches them, so the property passes vacuously on the hard cases. Inspecting and broadening the generator's distribution is essential.

questiontext.text: You check two individually-valid properties for one function. What is true about testing both together?

answer.text: Checking complementary properties strengthens the test — each rules out a different class of wrong implementations (e.g. "ordered" + "permutation" together pin down sort) — but even together they may not fully specify correctness

feedback.text: Correct — combining properties is stronger, yet not necessarily a complete specification.

answer.text: Combining two valid properties proves the function correct

feedback.text: No finite set of checks on sampled inputs proves correctness.

answer.text: You may only ever check one property per function

feedback.text: Multiple properties are encouraged and commonly used together.

answer.text: Combining two valid properties can make one of them false

feedback.text: Valid properties remain valid; checking them together does not invalidate either.

generalfeedback.text: Different properties catch different bug classes: "output is ordered" plus "output is a permutation of the input" together characterize a correct sort far better than either alone. Still, properties capture only the relations you thought of, and sampling is finite, so combining them raises confidence without proving correctness.

questiontext.text: How do property-based tests relate to hand-written example (unit) tests?

answer.text: They are complementary: properties cover a broad input space, while example tests pin down specific important cases, regressions, and known edge points — good suites use both

feedback.text: Correct — properties and examples reinforce each other.

answer.text: Property tests make example tests obsolete

feedback.text: Examples still document and lock down specific known cases and regressions.

answer.text: Example tests make property tests obsolete

feedback.text: Examples cover points; only properties explore a whole space of inputs.

answer.text: They test disjoint kinds of code and never overlap

feedback.text: They often test the same code from different angles; they are complementary, not disjoint.

generalfeedback.text: Example tests are precise, readable anchors for specific behaviors, boundary values, and past regressions. Property tests explore the space and surface surprises you did not think to write examples for. The strongest suites combine both rather than choosing one.

questiontext.text: During shrinking, a candidate reduced input no longer fails the property. What does the framework do?

answer.text: It discards that candidate and keeps shrinking from inputs that still fail; only an input that still triggers the failure is reported

feedback.text: Correct — shrinking keeps only still-failing candidates.

answer.text: It reports the passing reduced input as the counterexample

feedback.text: A passing input is not a counterexample and is never reported as one.

answer.text: It stops and declares the whole test passed

feedback.text: One passing shrink candidate does not clear the original failure.

answer.text: It modifies the property so the candidate fails

feedback.text: Shrinking never changes the property; it only reduces the input.

generalfeedback.text: Shrinking is a search constrained to still-failing inputs: any candidate that passes is rejected, and the search continues from ones that fail. The final reported counterexample therefore still violates the property, so the pass/fail verdict is unchanged — shrinking only makes the witness smaller.

name.text: Soundness condition for a round-trip property

questiontext.text: Under what condition is decode(encode(x)) == x a sound property (holding for every generated x)?

answer.text: When encode is injective and decode is a left inverse of encode on encode's range — i.e. decode undoes encode for every value x that can be generated

feedback.text: Correct — this is exactly what makes the round trip recover x.

answer.text: Always, for any encode and decode functions

feedback.text: If encode loses information (not injective), decoding cannot recover x.

answer.text: Only when encode and decode are the same function

feedback.text: They are inverses, generally different functions, not equal.

answer.text: Only when x is a string

feedback.text: The type of x is irrelevant; the inverse relationship is what matters.

generalfeedback.text: decode(encode(x)) == x requires encode to be injective (lossless) and decode to invert it on encode's outputs. If encode maps two distinct values to the same encoding, no decoder can recover both, so the property is unsound. Stating this condition is what keeps the round-trip property valid.

name.text: Choosing a model for a key-value store

questiontext.text: In model-based testing of a key-value store, what makes a good model to compare against?

answer.text: A simple in-memory dictionary whose behavior is obviously correct; after each generated command (put/get/delete) the store's observable result must match the dictionary's

feedback.text: Correct — a trivially-correct reference model is the ideal oracle.

answer.text: A second copy of the same store implementation

feedback.text: A copy shares the same bugs, so agreement proves nothing.

answer.text: A random oracle that returns arbitrary values

feedback.text: A random oracle has no defined correct behavior to compare against.

answer.text: The store's own performance counters

feedback.text: Performance counters are not a functional model of correctness.

generalfeedback.text: The model should be a minimal, obviously-correct abstraction (here, a plain dictionary). The point of model-based testing is to compare the complex real system against something simple enough to trust. Using a second copy of the real implementation would just duplicate its faults.

name.text: Why idempotence alone is a weak sort property

questiontext.text: Someone tests a sort function using only sort(sort(xs)) == sort(xs) (idempotence). Why is this weak?

answer.text: Many wrong functions are idempotent — e.g. one that always returns [], or the identity that returns xs unchanged — so idempotence does not require ordering or preservation of the input's elements

feedback.text: Correct — idempotence is satisfied by clearly incorrect sorts.

answer.text: Idempotence is false for a correct sort

feedback.text: It is true for a correct sort; it is just insufficient on its own.

answer.text: It fully verifies the sort by itself

feedback.text: It does not — wrong functions also pass it.

answer.text: It only fails on empty lists

feedback.text: It passes on empty lists too; the weakness is that wrong functions satisfy it.

generalfeedback.text: Both "always return []" and "return the input unchanged" satisfy sort(sort(xs)) == sort(xs), yet neither sorts. Idempotence is a genuine property of sort but a weak one; it must be combined with ordering and the permutation (multiset) condition to characterize correctness.

name.text: A weak generator range hides overflow

questiontext.text: A property about a 32-bit integer adder passes, but the generator only produces operands in [0, 100]. What is the best conclusion?

answer.text: The pass is weak evidence — overflow and boundary behavior near 2^31 were never generated, so the property was not exercised on the inputs most likely to fail

feedback.text: Correct — the risky inputs were never sampled, so confidence is limited.

answer.text: The adder is proven correct for all 32-bit inputs

feedback.text: Only tiny operands were tried; nothing is proven for large ones.

answer.text: Property-based testing is unsound

feedback.text: PBT is fine; the generator's range was simply too narrow.

answer.text: The property must be false

feedback.text: The property may be correct; it was just under-tested.

generalfeedback.text: Overflow bugs live near the type's extremes. A generator confined to [0, 100] cannot reach values near 2^31, so a clean run says nothing about the dangerous region. Widen the generator to include boundary and large values (and inspect its distribution) before trusting the result.

questiontext.text: A tester proposes reverse(xs) != xs for all lists (claiming reverse always changes the list). Why is this a bad property?

answer.text: It is false: palindromic lists, and the empty or single-element list, satisfy reverse(xs) == xs, so a correct reverse violates the proposed property — the property, not the code, is wrong

feedback.text: Correct — many lists are unchanged by reversal, so the "always changes" claim is false.

answer.text: It is correct and useful as written

feedback.text: It fails for palindromes and short lists, so it is not correct.

answer.text: It only fails for very long lists

feedback.text: It fails for the shortest lists (empty, single element) and any palindrome.

answer.text: reverse is not a pure function, so no property applies

feedback.text: reverse is pure; the issue is that the asserted property is simply false.

generalfeedback.text: The empty list, any single-element list, and every palindrome are unchanged by reversal, so reverse(xs) != xs does not hold universally. PBT would report one of these as a counterexample, exposing a flawed property rather than a defect. Always confirm a proposed property is genuinely necessary before trusting its failures.

name.text: What clean shrinking and a passing run establish

questiontext.text: After thousands of cases and clean shrinking on any failures encountered during development, all properties now pass. What can you conclude?

answer.text: No counterexample was found among the generated inputs; this raises confidence but does not prove the properties hold for all inputs, since the input space is usually unbounded

feedback.text: Correct — a clean run is strong evidence, not a proof.

answer.text: The program is now proven correct

feedback.text: Sampling finitely many inputs cannot prove a universal property.

answer.text: Every possible input has been tested

feedback.text: Only a finite random sample was tested, not the whole space.

answer.text: The properties are now mathematical theorems

feedback.text: Passing tests do not turn properties into proved theorems.

generalfeedback.text: PBT explores a sample of an often-infinite input space. A clean run — even with good generators and shrinking — means "no counterexample found here," which increases confidence but never amounts to a proof. For proof you would need formal verification, not testing.

questiontext.text: What is differential property-based testing?

answer.text: Generate random inputs and assert that two independent implementations of the same specification produce equal results; a disagreement is a counterexample locating a bug in (at least) one of them

feedback.text: Correct — differential testing cross-checks two implementations against each other.

answer.text: Comparing the running time of two implementations on random inputs

feedback.text: That is performance comparison, not differential correctness testing.

answer.text: Testing the arithmetic difference of two numbers

feedback.text: "Differential" here refers to comparing implementations, not subtracting numbers.

answer.text: Running one implementation twice with two different seeds

feedback.text: That checks determinism at best; differential testing compares two distinct implementations.

generalfeedback.text: Differential testing feeds the same generated inputs to two implementations of one spec (e.g. an optimized parser and a reference parser) and requires their outputs to match. Any disagreement, once shrunk to a minimal input, reveals a bug in one of them — provided at least one is trustworthy for that input.
